en: The Sūtra on the Turning of Existence, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of India during the Yuan Wei dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
In the forest, he was surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty, together with immeasurable and boundless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha departed from the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded to the Kalandakanivāpa bamboo grove.
Having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that King Bimbisāra was seated to one side, addressed him, saying: "Great King!
It is as if there were a man who, while in a dream, engaged in sexual acts with a precious woman; once he had awakened, he would still remember that precious woman."
"What do you think, Great King?
Does the woman-jewel in the dream exist? The king replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
He then asked the king again:
"Great King! What do you think?
If that person were to grasp at a woman in a dream, would he be considered wise?"
The king replied immediately:
“No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? Because that woman in the dream is ultimately non-existent, how could there be any objective reality for the act of desire?
That person’s efforts are merely in vain.
The Buddha said, "Great King! It is so;
all foolish worldlings, because they have never heard the True Dharma of the Buddha, see various forms with their eyes and, their minds becoming delighted, immediately grasp them as real."
Due to attachment, there is bondage; due to bondage, there is clinging;
and due to clinging, the karmas of greed, hatred, and delusion arise.

Whether it be actions of body, speech, or mind, the bodily action performed ceases immediately; having ceased, it does not abide in the eastern direction, nor does it abide in the southern, western, northern, upward, or downward directions. At the time of death, that consciousness with its objective support (*sāśraya-vijñāna*) undergoes transformation and manifests as the subsequent mind.
"Great King!
That consciousness is not destroyed; wherever karma is exhausted, that very karma can manifest, just like a precious woman appearing upon waking from a dream.
Thus it is, Great King!"

Finally, as the preceding consciousness ceases, a subsequent consciousness arises—whether in hell, among the hungry ghosts, among animals, among the asuras, among humans, or among devas. That final consciousness grasps that final birth, and the consciousness conforms to that rebirth.
"In this way, consciousness follows what is experienced through karma; yet there is no dharma that transmigrates from this world to another world to undergo rebirth.
O Great King!"
The cessation of the final consciousness is called "cessation. This initial consciousness is like one who takes rebirth; it is the subsequent birth.
Your Majesty!
When the final consciousness passes away, those phenomena do not actually come from that place to arrive here; once the initial consciousness has arisen, it likewise goes nowhere.
Why is this? Because it is the characteristic of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Great King!

The final consciousness is empty of final consciousness; karma is empty of karma; birth is empty of birth; the initial consciousness is empty of initial consciousness; and the place of birth is empty of the place of birth, yet within that place, the fruits of karma are not lost.
"Great King!

The consciousness of the final birth ceases right there; yet the subsequent mind is not severed, for the consciousness-mind proceeds in accordance with its course, going wherever it must to receive the karmic retribution it has incurred."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“When the Sugata speaks later, All the words he utters Are spoken as mere conventional designations, For they abide by way of conventional conceptualization.”
Detached from the nature of language, there is nothing that can be spoken;
yet, in accordance with whatever speech exists, one speaks of those various phenomena.
They do not reside therein; the eye of Dharma sees them as formless.
What is called "seeing forms" arises from worldly attachment; thus one speaks of worldly phenomena as real.
Yet they are seen through a combination of what does not exist—this is what the Tathāgata has taught, and it is called the stage of skillful means.
If one speaks according to ultimate truth, the eye does not see forms and the mind does not know phenomena; this is the most profound secret.
What the world calls "I" and "mine" is by nature empty and nameless.
"All dharmas are nameless, yet they are spoken of by means of provisional names.

When this Dharma-gate was being taught, King Bimbisāra, along with the great assembly—humans, devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, and others—hearing what the Buddha had said, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
The Sūtra on the Transformation of Existence Spoken by the Buddha
